title: TriageIQ: an AI support inbox that sorts tickets and drafts grounded replies, fully on-device

scenes.title: TriageIQ: overview
lines: Project three: TriageIQ.
A support inbox that reads every email, sorts it by category, priority and mood, and drafts a reply from tickets you've already solved.
It all runs on one laptop, with a local language model, so customer text never leaves the machine. Built with Python, Kafka, Ollama, Qdrant, FastAPI and Docker.

scenes.title: The problem
lines: A support inbox fills up with everything: refunds, crashes, password resets, angry customers, and thank you notes, all mixed together.
Someone has to read each one, decide how urgent it is, and write a reply.
Meanwhile, the angry email about a double charge can sit behind fifty routine questions.

scenes.title: The pipeline
lines: TriageIQ is an event-driven pipeline. A gateway reads the inbox over IMAP, and turns each new email into a ticket on a Kafka topic.
A consumer classifies it with a local LLM, drafts a reply with RAG, and publishes the result to a second topic.
A FastAPI console streams those tickets live to the support agent.
And replies go back out over SMTP, but only after a human approves.

scenes.title: Why Kafka
lines: Why Kafka in the middle? It decouples the steps. If the model is slow, emails pile up safely in the topic, instead of being lost.
And the consumer group remembers how far it has read, so after a restart, it carries on from exactly the same place.

scenes.title: Step 1: Classify with a local LLM
lines: Step one: classify. The model is Qwen 2.5, with three billion parameters, running locally in Ollama.
The prompt defines every category and priority precisely, and a JSON schema forces the answer into exactly three fields, each from a fixed list.
Temperature is zero, so the same email always gets the same answer.

scenes.title: Never trust the model blindly
lines: And it never trusts the model blindly. If Ollama is down, times out, or returns anything that isn't valid, the ticket isn't dropped.
It falls back to needs human, with high priority, so a person looks at it first.
Here's that fallback, running for real, with the model switched off.

scenes.title: Step 2: RAG over past tickets
lines: Step two: draft a reply with RAG. Thirty past tickets, and how they were solved, are embedded with nomic embed text, and stored in Qdrant.
A new ticket is embedded the same way, and Qdrant returns the three most similar past tickets, by cosine similarity.
Anything below a similarity of 0.55 is ignored. If nothing is similar enough, there's no draft, and a human answers instead.

scenes.title: Grounded replies
lines: The prompt says: use only the facts in those past answers. Never invent policies, amounts, or time frames.
If they don't fully answer the customer, say a team member will follow up.
That's what grounded means: the model writes the words, but the facts come from your own history.

scenes.title: Step 3: Human in the loop
lines: Step three: a human stays in the loop. The console streams every ticket over Server-Sent Events.
The agent can approve the draft, edit it, write their own, or send it to a human.
Only when they approve does the email go out, over SMTP, in the same thread, using In-Reply-To and References headers.

scenes.title: Hardened for a real inbox
lines: It's hardened for a real inbox. Every email's Message-ID is stored, so the same email never becomes two tickets.
Auto-replies, bulk mail, mailing lists, bounces and no-reply senders are skipped. That stops two auto-responders from replying to each other forever.
One sender can create at most five tickets an hour. And the console uses a signed session cookie, with a lockout after six wrong passwords in ten minutes.

scenes.title: Demo: the console
lines: Here's the console. The overview shows how many tickets are waiting, by priority.
In the approval queue, each ticket shows its category, priority and mood, the customer's message, and the AI's draft, ready to approve.
And the system page shows how tickets travel through the pipeline.
This is demo mode, so these tickets and AI results are simulated.

scenes.title: Honest limits
lines: The honest limits. The knowledge base is thirty hand-written, synthetic tickets, so draft quality on real company data is untested.
Accuracy hasn't been formally measured yet. And a small three billion parameter model is fast and private, but less accurate than a large hosted one.
Next steps: a labelled evaluation set, and monitoring of model latency and errors.

scenes.title: Recap
lines: Reads it. Ranks it. Drafts the reply.
And nothing is sent until a human approves.
